title: State Corporate Tax Rates Decline 33% Since 1980s - ALEC-Driven 'Race to Bottom' Shifts Tax Burden from Corporations to Working Families
summary: By 2019, average state corporate income tax rates had declined approximately 33% from their 1980s levels, reflecting decades of systematic tax-cutting campaigns driven primarily by the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) and coordinated corporate lobbying efforts. This 'race to the bottom' accelerated dramatically after ALEC's 2007 publication of 'Rich States, Poor States'—an annual report co-authored by supply-side economist Arthur Laffer that ranks states based on tax levels and regulations, explicitly designed to pressure states into competitive tax cutting. The report's methodology is fundamentally flawed: it assumes lower taxes and fewer regulations automatically produce better economic outcomes, when empirical research consistently shows states that conform less to ALEC's policy prescriptions actually achieve better results for job creation and wage growth. Nevertheless, ALEC's coordinated lobbying infrastructure—bringing together state legislators, corporate lobbyists, and think tank operatives at lavish conferences to draft model legislation—has successfully convinced Republican-controlled state legislatures to implement wave after wave of corporate tax cuts. Between 2012 and 2019, states including Kansas, North Carolina, Wisconsin, Ohio, Michigan, and Indiana slashed corporate tax rates, often simultaneously cutting individual income taxes while increasing sales taxes and fees that disproportionately burden low-income families. The cumulative effect has been massive: corporate share of state tax revenues declined substantially while working families' share increased, even as corporate profits reached record levels. States justified cuts using ALEC's 'economic competitiveness' framing, claiming lower corporate taxes would attract businesses and create jobs—promises that rarely materialized. Instead, states experienced revenue shortfalls forcing cuts to education, healthcare, infrastructure, and other essential services. The race to the bottom created perverse incentives: states that maintained adequate corporate tax rates to fund public services were pressured by ALEC's rankings and corporate threats of relocation, while states offering the lowest rates attracted businesses that then demanded further concessions. This dynamic exemplifies systematic capture: ALEC provides the ideological justification, model legislation, and political pressure infrastructure; corporations fund ALEC and donate to legislators who implement the cuts; and the tax burden shifts from profitable corporations to working families, small businesses, and consumption-based taxes. The state-level race to the bottom complemented federal corporate tax cuts, creating a comprehensive tax avoidance infrastructure that allowed the most profitable corporations in history to pay effective tax rates far below statutory rates.
